title: The Vine and the Burned Branches
hook: When Jesus says fruitless branches are thrown into the fire, is he describing hell?
tldr: John 15 uses a familiar vineyard scene: dead cuttings were piled up and burned. The vine was Israel's ancient symbol, and the prophets pictured God's fruitless vine burned and cut down in national disaster. The point is fruitfulness through staying joined to Jesus. Neither the vine, the fire nor the gatherers are linked to an afterlife of torment.
big_idea: Burned branches are a vineyard picture of fruitlessness, not a map of hell.

points.title: Israel was God's vine
points.text: Psalm 80, Isaiah 5 and Jeremiah 2:21 picture Israel as a vine God planted and tended, which produced wild grapes. When Jesus says 'I am the true vine,' he claims to be what Israel was meant to be.

points.title: Prunings really were burned
points.text: In vineyards, cut and dead branches were bundled and burned as waste. Gary Derickson's study of first-century viticulture notes branches were removed, piled up and burned at season's end. Jesus' hearers would picture a farm bonfire.

points.title: Vine wood is only good to burn
points.text: Ezekiel 15 asks what vine wood is good for: not even a peg. A fruitless vine is fit only for fuel, and Ezekiel applies this to Jerusalem's coming destruction by Babylon, a historical judgment.

points.title: The subject is fruit
points.text: The passage repeats 'fruit' again and again: the Father prunes branches to bear more, and the disciples glorify him by bearing much fruit. The warning serves that goal; it says nothing about souls after death.

points.title: Readers who reject hell disagree
points.text: Some read the fire as temporal discipline (Jeremy Myers, Grace Evangelical Society). Others see Israel's branches cut off before AD 70, consumed (annihilation) or purified. All agree the image is not unending torment.

points.title: Paul's fire burns works
points.text: In 1 Corinthians 3 the fire tests what believers built. Bad work burns up, yet the builder is saved 'as through fire.' Hebrews 6 pictures a weedy field burned, a farming practice that cleared land.

sections.summary: Jesus speaks to his eleven disciples on the night before his death, after the Last Supper. He says he is the true vine, the Father is the vinedresser, and they are the branches. The theme is abiding: remaining joined to him. Apart from him they can do nothing; joined to him they bear much fruit and prove to be his disciples.

Psalm 80 says God brought a vine out of Egypt, planted it, and later it was burned with fire and cut down. Isaiah 5 sings of a vineyard that yielded wild grapes, whose hedge God removes. Jeremiah 2:21 says God planted a choice vine that became a wild one. Hosea and Ezekiel use the same picture. 'True vine' contrasts Jesus with that failed vine.

Ezekiel asks whether vine wood can make even a peg to hang a pot. It cannot; it is thrown into the fire as fuel, and once charred it is even less useful. God applies this to the people of Jerusalem, about five years before Babylon destroyed the city. The fire is a national catastrophe in history.

In John 15:2 the Father 'takes away' (airō) every branch without fruit. The verb can also mean lift up. Some commentators say vinedressers lifted trailing branches off the ground so they could dry and bear fruit. Marg Mowczko notes that English translations all render it 'removes'. Either way, the Father's work aims at fruit.

John 15:6 says a branch that does not abide is thrown away, withers, and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire and burned. The verbs 'they gather' and 'they throw' have no named subject; the KJV supplies 'men'. Derickson's viticulture study describes cut branches piled up and burned at season's end. Burning ends the branch; it does not keep it burning.

sections.h: What the fire means: the options
sections.summary: Coffman and older commentators read the fire as the final fate of the wicked. Verse By Verse Commentary and Grace Evangelical Society see temporal judgment on unfruitful lives. Myers calls it temporal discipline, leaving a heap of ash. Others read branches as Israelites cut off, as Romans 11 says broken branches can be grafted back in.

Paul says each builder's work will be tested by fire on the Day. Gold, silver and precious stones survive; wood, hay and straw burn. If someone's work is burned up, he suffers loss, yet he himself is saved, 'but only as through fire.' Catholics see purgatory here; evangelicals see works tested; some fathers saw a fire all must pass through.

Hebrews 6 compares people to land: land that drinks the rain and yields a crop receives blessing; land that yields thorns and thistles is worthless and its end is to be burned. Commentators note farmers burned barren land and stubble to destroy weeds. One commentator observes burning was remedial in farming, clearing the way for new growth.

parable.audience: The eleven disciples in the Upper Room, the night before the crucifixion.
parable.setting: Jesus' farewell discourse after the Last Supper. Vineyards filled the land, and the vine was Israel's national emblem in the prophets. He prepares his followers to continue his work after he leaves.

decoder.traditional: Christ as source of individual salvation.
decoder.original: Jesus as the faithful Israel, contrasted with the fruitless vine of Psalm 80, Isaiah 5 and Jeremiah 2:21.

decoder.traditional: God the judge who removes the unsaved.
decoder.original: The Father as a farmer, tending, lifting and pruning so that branches bear more fruit.

decoder.traditional: Proof of genuine faith, required to escape hell.
decoder.original: The life and works that flow from abiding in Jesus: love, obedience, answered prayer, and glory to the Father.
A life cut off from its source, as Israel's branches were broken off in Romans 11, yet able to be grafted back.

decoder.traditional: Cast into the eternal fire of hell.
decoder.original: The normal fate of vineyard prunings: piled and burned as waste. Fire consumes and ends; in Ezekiel 15 it meant Jerusalem's historical fall.

visuals.title: Reading John 15:6 slowly
visuals.text: If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.

notes.note: An explicit simile. Jesus compares a life to a vineyard branch; he is not describing a place.
Cut off from sap, the branch dries out. Death of fruitfulness is the first result.
Greek 'they gather' has no named subject; vineyard workers piled the cuttings.
Burning consumes dry wood quickly. Nothing in the verse says the branches keep burning forever.

mythfact.myth: John 15:6 is one of Jesus' clear descriptions of hell.
mythfact.fact: It is an explicit simile ('like a branch') from vineyard life. The fire is never named or located, and the passage's concern is bearing fruit, not where souls go after death.

mythfact.myth: Fire in Scripture always means the afterlife.
mythfact.fact: The vine imagery behind John 15 uses fire for history: Psalm 80's vine burned and cut down, and Ezekiel 15's vine wood representing Jerusalem's fall to Babylon.

mythfact.myth: Fruitless believers will be sent to hell.
mythfact.fact: Jeremy Myers answers 'NO!' and many evangelical commentators read loss or discipline. Paul says a builder whose work burns still 'will be saved, but only as through fire.'

quiz.q: Which Old Testament image lies behind 'I am the true vine'?
quiz.why: Psalm 80, Isaiah 5 and Jeremiah 2:21 picture Israel as the vine God planted that failed to bear good fruit.

quiz.q: What does Ezekiel 15 say vine wood is good for?
quiz.why: It cannot make even a peg. Ezekiel applies this to Jerusalem's judgment by Babylon.
The work is burned and the builder suffers loss, yet he himself is saved as through fire.

objections.claim: Being thrown into the fire and burned is the language of hell, as in Matthew 13 where angels gather the wicked into the furnace.
objections.strongest: Coffman and others note the striking parallel: gathering, throwing into fire, burning. Jesus used the same pattern for final judgment in Matthew 13:40-42. A branch cut off from Christ is an unbeliever, and unbelievers face the eternal fire.
objections.response: John never mentions angels, the end of the age, or furnaces; the Greek 'they gather' has no named subject, and the scene matches ordinary vineyard practice of piling and burning cuttings. The scriptural background is Psalm 80 and Ezekiel 15, where Israel the vine is burned in historical disasters. And even if final judgment is meant, branches that are burned are consumed, not kept alive in fire. The image supports destruction or loss, not conscious torment.

objections.claim: If believers cannot lose salvation, the branches must be false believers headed for hell.
objections.strongest: Many Reformed readers argue the cut-off branches never truly abided. Their fruitlessness proves they were never saved, so the fire is the hell that awaits all unbelievers, including religious pretenders like Judas.
objections.response: This reading imports hell to solve a theological puzzle. Jesus addresses his own disciples, and the passage's stated aim is fruit and the Father's glory. Grace Evangelical Society notes James Montgomery Boice linked the burning with useless works destroyed rather than loss of salvation. Paul makes that very distinction: a believer's works can burn while he is saved through fire. And Romans 11 shows broken-off branches can be grafted in again, so being cut off is not necessarily final.

objections.claim: Hebrews 6:8 says the field's end is to be burned under a curse; that is final damnation for apostates.
objections.strongest: Hebrews 6:4-6 warns that those who fall away cannot be restored to repentance. Verse 8's curse and burning naturally describe the eternal judgment of apostates, a judicial visitation of the severest kind.
objections.response: The picture is agricultural: farmers burned weedy, barren land, as Pliny describes for stubble, to destroy weeds. One commentator notes such burning was remedial rather than punitive, restoring the field. Hebrews' fire falls on thorns and thistles, the bad growth, not on the land as a living sufferer. Like John 15 it warns about fruitlessness in vivid farm terms; it does not say anyone burns forever.
